vol_risk_premium.title: The variance risk premium: why options usually cost more than they 'should'
body: If implied vol were a pure forecast, it would sit above realized vol about half the time and below it the other half. It doesn't: across decades of index data, implied vol has been above subsequently realized vol most of the time, by a few points on average. That persistent gap is the variance risk premium (VRP).

The premium exists because option sellers are insuring other investors against crashes, and crashes arrive exactly when everyone's wealth is falling. Bearing that risk deserves compensation, the same way an insurer charges more than expected claims. Systematic put-selling strategies earn the VRP most years and then give back a large chunk in events like 2008, Feb 2018 or March 2020 — the payoff profile is 'pick up nickels in front of a steamroller'.

So 'IV above realized' is the normal state, and only a large or unusual gap is a signal. When IV falls below realized, either the market expects things to calm down or options are genuinely cheap relative to the movement on offer.

event_pricing.title: Reading an event straight out of the term structure
body: Total implied variance (σ²T) adds up across time. If the market expects a normal day to carry variance v and an earnings day to carry an extra jump J², the expiry just after the event has total variance ≈ v·T + J². That's why the vol of the first post-event expiry is lifted, and the lift fades for longer expiries as the jump gets diluted across more days.

Subtracting adjacent expiries' total variance isolates the window that contains the event (forward variance). Remove the 'normal' variance from that window and the square root of what's left is the implied event move — the same number desks quote as 'the market is pricing a ±X% move on earnings'.
After the event, that jump variance disappears overnight: the 'vol crush'. Option owners who were right about direction can still lose money if the stock moves less than the implied move.

spot_vol.title: Spot-vol correlation: why vol usually rises when stocks fall
body: Equity implied vol is negatively correlated with price. Two reasons: the leverage effect (a falling stock price raises a firm's debt-to-equity, making the equity riskier) and the demand side (when markets fall, investors rush to buy puts, and dealers who sell them raise prices).

Traders summarize this with the spot-vol beta — vol points of change per 1% move in the price. For broad indexes it's typically a few tenths to around one vol point per 1%, steeper in selloffs. It's also why skew exists: if vol will be higher after a drop, low strikes deserve higher implied vol today.

Days where price and vol move together are the interesting ones. Both up usually means demand for upside — a squeeze, a takeover rumor, a hype rally where calls get bid. Both down often means a known event has passed and its premium is draining out even as the stock slips.

skew.title: Skew: what the smile says about crash fear
body: Before the 1987 crash, index smiles were nearly flat. Afterward, out-of-the-money puts have permanently carried higher implied vols than calls the same distance away. The market learned that the left tail is fatter than a lognormal model assumes.

The 25-delta risk reversal (call vol minus put vol) is the standard skew measure; dividing by ATM vol makes it comparable across tickers and regimes. A steeper skew means hedging is getting more expensive relative to the overall vol level — a sign of rising concern even if ATM vol hasn't moved.

Single stocks can show the opposite — call skew — when the upside is the bigger risk to shorts (a meme rally, a takeover target, a hot AI name). That's the market telling you which tail people are scrambling to own.

term_inversion.title: When the term structure inverts
body: Normally longer-dated options carry higher vol than short-dated ones: more can happen over a longer horizon, and short-dated vol mean-reverts toward a long-run level. That upward slope is called contango.

When near-dated vol rises above longer-dated (backwardation), the market expects the next few weeks to be rougher than the long-run average. It happens in selloffs — the VIX curve famously inverts in crises — and right before a known event like earnings or a Fed decision.

Because vol mean-reverts, an inverted curve is also a forecast that things will calm down later. Traders watch the slope as a stress gauge: a flip from contango to backwardation is often more informative than the level of vol itself.

gamma_theta.title: Gamma vs theta: the rent you pay to own convexity
body: An option owner is long gamma: as the stock moves, delta moves in their favor, so big moves in either direction make money. The price of that convexity is theta — the option loses value every day the stock sits still.

In Black-Scholes the two are tied together: for a delta-hedged option, the daily P&L is approximately ½·Γ·S²·(realized daily variance − implied daily variance). Put simply, the owner wins if the stock moves more than implied vol predicted, and the seller wins if it moves less. Theta is just the implied side of that equation, paid in advance.

This is why 'is vol cheap or expensive?' is really the question 'will the stock move more or less than the market is charging for?' — the comparison the market read makes with implied vs realized vol.

expected_move.title: Turning a vol number into a price range
body: Implied vol is an annualized standard deviation of returns. Scaling by √time converts it to any horizon: σ·√(days/365) for calendar days, or σ/√252 for one trading day. Multiply by the price and you get the dollar range the market expects about two-thirds of the time.
The √time rule comes from returns being roughly independent day to day, so variances add. It's why a 16% annual vol is a ~1% daily vol (16/√252 ≈ 1.0) — the trader's 'rule of 16'.

The range is a one-standard-deviation band under a normal distribution. Real returns have fatter tails, so moves of 2-3× the band happen more often than the textbook ~5% and ~0.3% — which is exactly what skew and the butterfly are pricing.

early_exercise.title: Why American puts are worth more than European puts
body: An American option can be exercised any day before expiry. For a call on a non-dividend stock that right is worthless — you'd always rather sell the call than exercise it. For a put it can be valuable: exercising a deep in-the-money put hands you the strike in cash today, and that cash earns interest.

The binomial tree values the right by checking, at every node, whether exercising beats holding. Longstaff-Schwartz does the same with Monte Carlo paths, using a regression to estimate the value of holding. Both should land near each other; Black-Scholes can't, because it only prices European exercise.

The premium grows with interest rates, time to expiry and how far in the money the put is. At the money with short expiries it's usually a few cents — small, but real money for market makers quoting thousands of contracts.

lesson.title: Gamma vs theta: the rent you pay to own convexity
lesson.worked: PLTR today: the $162 put has gamma 0.0295 and theta -0.366. A typical one-day move of ±3.45% ($5.58) earns a delta-hedged owner about ½·Γ·dS² = $0.460, against $0.366 of decay per calendar day. A trading day earns more than one day's theta, but weekends charge decay with no trading: five trading days of gamma roughly pay for seven calendar days of theta — break-even when the stock moves exactly as implied.

learn.iv_rv: Implied vol (IV) is the market's forecast of how much the stock will move, backed out of option prices. Realized vol is how much it actually moved. Option sellers usually demand IV a bit above realized — the 'variance risk premium' — as payment for insuring big moves. A large gap means options are expensive relative to recent behavior (or the market expects something); IV below realized means options are cheap unless things calm down.
learn.expected_move: A rough one-standard-deviation range: price × IV × √(days/365). About two-thirds of the time the stock should finish inside it, if the market's vol is right. It's how traders translate a vol number into dollars.
learn.skew: The 25-delta risk reversal compares a 25-delta call's vol with a 25-delta put's vol (25-delta ≈ the option has a 25% chance of finishing in the money). Negative means puts cost more. Equities almost always have put skew: investors pay for crash protection, and stocks tend to get more volatile when they fall (the 'leverage effect').
learn.butterfly: The 25-delta butterfly is the average wing vol minus ATM vol — how much curvature the smile has. Bigger means the market is paying extra for large moves in either direction, i.e. it's pricing fatter tails than a normal distribution.
learn.term: The term structure plots ATM IV against time to expiry. Normally it slopes up ('contango') because more can happen over longer horizons and sellers want more for longer risk. When near-dated vol sits above longer-dated ('backwardation' / inverted), the market expects trouble soon — typical during selloffs or right before a known event.
learn.forward_vol: Forward vol is the vol the market implies for the window between two expiries: sqrt((σ₂²T₂ − σ₁²T₁)/(T₂ − T₁)). Total variance (σ²T) adds up over time, so subtracting isolates one window. A window far above its neighbors means a specific event, like earnings, is priced inside it.
learn.event_move: Strip out the 'normal' daily vol from the event window and what's left is the jump the market prices for the event itself. This is how desks estimate the implied earnings move straight from the term structure.
learn.smile_sides: Comparing options the same distance from the money on each side (here one standard deviation, ±σ√T) shows which tail the market fears more. Measuring in standard deviations rather than dollars makes short and long expiries comparable.
learn.smirk: Equity smiles usually bottom out slightly above the forward price, not at it: vol falls as strikes rise until the call wing starts to curl back up. That lopsided shape is called a 'smirk' and is the visual form of put skew.
learn.fit: Each expiry is fitted with SVI (Stochastic Volatility Inspired, Gatheral 2004), a five-parameter curve for total variance that traders use because it fits real smiles well and makes arbitrage easy to check. RMSE is the average gap between the curve and quotes.
learn.arbitrage: Static arbitrage checks: the 'butterfly' condition (the implied probability density can't go negative) and the 'calendar' condition (total variance can't fall as expiry lengthens). Flags on adjacent weekly expiries often come from weekends — time is measured in calendar days but markets don't move on Saturdays — and flags just after an earnings expiry come from the event's variance dropping out of the later smile's wings. Small flags like these are data texture, not free money: bid/ask spreads are wider.
learn.american: American options can be exercised early. For a put, early exercise can make sense when it's deep in the money (you collect the strike now and earn interest on it). The binomial tree and Longstaff-Schwartz both value that right; Black-Scholes can't, so the gap between the American and European prices is the early-exercise premium.
learn.models_agree: Black-Scholes is exact for European options under its assumptions. The binomial tree and Monte Carlo are numerical methods that should converge to it — a tree within a fraction of a cent and Monte Carlo within ~2 standard errors means both are working.
learn.history: Comparing to the engine's own saved history shows whether today is unusual for this ticker, which is more meaningful than comparing different stocks' vol levels.
learn.daily_move: Dividing an annual vol by √252 (trading days) gives the typical one-day move it implies. Comparing that with what the stock actually did tells you whether option buyers or sellers 'won' the day: a move bigger than implied rewards owners of options (long gamma), a smaller one rewards the sellers who collected time decay.
learn.spot_vol: For most stocks, implied vol rises when the price falls and eases when it rallies — fear shows up as demand for puts, and falling stocks really do get more volatile. The ratio of vol change to price change is the 'spot-vol beta'. When price and vol move the same way, something unusual is happening: a squeeze or hype rally (both up), or event vol draining out of a falling stock (both down).
learn.greeks_dollars: Greeks translate risk into dollars. Delta: price change per $1 move in the stock. Gamma: how much delta itself changes per $1. Theta: what one calendar day costs the owner. Vega: what one vol point is worth. Quotes are per share; one contract is 100 shares.
